title: Jen:
title_q: “For the First Time in My Life I Reached Out”
title_short: Jen · First Time I Reached Out
headline: She wanted to relapse and had never asked anyone for help. A peer at Honu made it safe. Now she works there.
story: Jen came to Honu House straight out of prison, as a guest. She wanted to use again. She had never been a person who asks for help. A peer at the house made it feel safe, and for the first time in her life she reached out. Today she works at Honu.
This is MHA's idea in one person: a peer, not a degree, made the difference. It must feel warm and hopeful. Her hard moment is one honest beat. The video ends on “we do recover.”
do: Open on frame 1 with “for the first time in my life…”. Hook text on frame 1.
Stay on her face when she talks about wanting to use.
Super says Honu House. The B-roll is Keya. Never put “Honu” on a Keya shot.
Use the second take of the peer support answer (01:55), not the first.
dont: No logo, name or title card at 0:00.
Nothing about house rules or “enforcing rules” (04:46–05:14).
No dark music, no slow motion, no prison images.
Do not use her standalone “peer support is powerful” lines. They break and restart.

transcript:
Auto-transcript of 20260909_C4696.MP4 (Jen, Honu House staff, filmed at Keya House, Lincoln, 9 Sep 2026). Times are mm:ss in the source file. Speaker labels removed: many are wrong. The interviewer is off camera.
[00:00] (Before the interview: chair and phone, 00:00–00:11.)
[00:15] (Interviewer) So we're gonna start with you introducing yourself, so your name, your position, and how long you've been at MHA.
[00:22] My name is Jen.
[00:24] I work at the Honu House, and I have been working there for two months.
[00:30] Previously, before that, I volunteered for about three to four months.
[00:36] (Interviewer) So how did you first come across MHA?
[00:39] I actually came across MHA when I had came out of prison, and it was my transitional living from coming out of prison before I would transition on to completely my own.
[00:52] So I came to that house for three months after I had gotten out of incarceration.
[01:00] (Interviewer) What makes peer support different from traditional peer support in your experience at Honu?
[01:06] (First try and restart, 01:06–01:49.)
[01:50] (Interviewer) What makes peer support different than traditional support you've received in the past?
[01:56] Peer support is way different than what I would consider clinical support because it is a person that is...
[02:04] They don't have any special degree or anything like that, but they have life experiences that may relate to you so they can give their feedback on how they got through a situation or how they handled it, which is, I feel like, a lot more useful because someone just learning out of a book by education is not the same as relating to a person.
[02:29] So it gives them a whole another perspective and I feel like it supports people way more successfully with that.
[02:39] I mean, that's what did the difference for me when I first got peer support.
[02:44] (Interviewer) So is there any moments or memories that you still think about either as a guest or as an employee at MHA?
[02:52] I would have to refer to when I was a guest and I have addiction issues, I'm a recovering drug addict, and I was living at the HONU house and I was wanting to relapse, I was wanting to use.
[03:10] And I have never in my life been a person who easily reaches out for help or I've never known how to go about that, I've never even wanted to for that matter because of trust issues and other things.
[03:25] And because of a connection I had made with one of the peer support specialists at the HONU house, for the first time in my life, I was actually able to reach out for help and I felt comfortable to do that because the people that work at the house, they are very approachable, they make you feel at ease, like it was comfortable for the first time in my life, where I didn't, I felt safe and I felt I could speak about things and it would be okay.
[03:58] And because of that, I've been successful in my recovery and I wouldn't be where I am today.
[04:04] I wouldn't be working here and I wouldn't be sober and it completely changed my life.
[04:10] (Interviewer) Thank you for sharing that. What would you say to someone who doesn't believe that they can recover?
[04:16] I would say all you need is to want it.
[04:20] If you want it, then there's support out there like us, for instance, and if I can do it, anybody can do it, as long as they reach out for that support, because it is possible, we do recover.
[04:35] And there's proof in a lot of the people I work with or that I'm surrounded with at MHA.
[04:42] (Interviewer) What do people get wrong about this work?
[04:46] I think when people think and they don't know about, for instance, like the Honu House, they think like the staff there are just staff, like they're there to tell you what to do, they're there to enforce the rules.
[05:00] And yes, we do have to enforce rules to a certain extent, but we're just, the people that work for MHA work there because they have a passion for it.
[05:09] They actually care about the people that are living there and that they're working with.
[05:14] They literally, they want to do it, it's out of their, because they feel, okay, I got to start all over again.
[05:22] (Interviewer) You can start over. ... You could just start from like they want to do this job from passion or whatever.
[05:32] Yeah, they do this job out of compassion and for caring about these people.
[05:36] It's not just a job for most of us, I would say for any of us.
[05:40] It's hard to even call it a job because I'm so, I go to work and I, it's like I'm having just conversations with my friends and I'm just having, you know, it's just, it's like stuttering now.
[05:55] (Crew: that was really good, the beauty of editing.)
[06:01] (Interviewer) If someone watching has never heard of MHA, what should they know?
[06:07] They should know that it's a, what would we call... it's not a company. Organization.
[06:22] I would say it's an organization that makes a big difference in people's lives and it changes everything because it's got support that I have never seen anywhere else in my life.
[06:34] It's a whole different level of support and you're going to get the assistance.
[06:40] We walk like beside people through their struggles and like when they have goals or struggles, whichever, whatever it may be that is their, where they want to be in their life or what they see as their life being like they want it, we just stand by their sides and walk through that with them just trying to kind of guiding them, showing them maybe what the things are that is out there that will help them get to those goals or they'll get through those struggles.
[07:13] We're there through all that, we just support them.
[07:21] (Interviewer) So we're going to do some standalone lines. So the first one is just my name is Jen and I work at Honu at MHA.
[07:30] My name is Jen and I work at Honu through MHA. (Repeated at 07:36.)
[07:42] (Interviewer) And then one sentence on what hope looks like to you now.
[07:47] Hope to me is seeing that there is a light at the end of the tunnel and that there is a room to get through whatever you're going through.
[07:59] (Interviewer) And then peer support is powerful because.
[08:13] Peer support is powerful because you have somebody that is wanting to walk by your side and help you get, sorry. I can't say help, I gotta say support.
[08:37] Peer support is powerful because you have somebody who has passion and they care and they want to walk by your side and support you through your struggles and to get to where you wanna be.
[08:51] And there's no other career or I don't know how to say that in part. Like, there's no other.
[09:09] I don't think there's any other support out there like the intentional peer support. Like it's unique and it's special and it's different than any other type of support that you can find out there for a resource.
[09:22] (Wrap-up chat, 09:22–09:40.)
